Samuel Davies
sam'yōo-êl dā'vis
n. (Samuel Davies, 1723–1761, evangelist of Virginia Presbyterianism, hymnwriter, President of the College of New Jersey)
Welsh patronymic, son of David; Samuel, from Hebrew Shemu'el, heard of God.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Samuel Davies was trained at Samuel Blair's school at Fagg's Manor and sent in 1747 as an evangelist to Hanover County, Virginia, where the established church held the ground and dissenters preached by licence or not at all. He secured licences for seven meeting houses, argued the legal case for toleration under the Act of Toleration before the General Court, and built the first Presbyterian presbytery in the colony. He catechized and taught slaves to read so that they could read the Scriptures, baptized many, and left accounts of their singing that are among the earliest notices of African-American Christian worship. In 1753 he sailed with Gilbert Tennent to raise money in Britain for the College of New Jersey, and became its president in 1759, dying eighteen months later at thirty-seven. Rom 10:14 drove the whole: how shall they hear without a preacher. Act 26:18 names the commission he worked under, to turn men from darkness to light.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an evangelist as a preacher or publisher of the gospel; and toleration, as the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state.

expand to see more

EVAN'GELIST, n. A writer of the history of Jesus Christ; a preacher or publisher of the gospel of Jesus Christ.

TOLERA'TION, n. The allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to those of the established church.

CAT'ECHIZE, v.t. To instruct by asking questions, receiving answers, and offering explanations and corrections.

Key Scripture

Rom 10:14 — "How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?"

Act 26:18 — "To open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins, and inheritance among them which are sanctified by faith that is in me."

Rom 10:15 — "And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!"

Psa 119:130 — "The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple."

Modern Corruption

He won legal room for dissenters in Virginia and spent it teaching slaves to read the Bible.

expand to see more

Davies is the answer to the claim that colonial Reformed Christianity had nothing to say to the enslaved. He taught reading because Psa 119:130 is true, that the entrance of God's words giveth light and giveth understanding unto the simple, and a man who cannot read cannot enter them for himself. He baptized on profession after examination, the same standard he applied to planters, which in that society was itself a statement.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest thing to say is that Davies did not call for abolition and that the dictionary does not pretend he did. What he did was refuse the premise on which the whole system leaned, that these were not souls to be addressed. Act 26:18 commissions the turning of men from darkness to light and from the power of Satan unto God, and it names no exempt category. The principle to recover is that literacy in the Scriptures is a missionary act.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kerusso (G2784), to preach; epistrepho (G1994), to turn; Hebrew pethach (H6608), opening, entrance.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to herald, to preach; Romans 10:14.

Greek akouo (G191) — to hear; Romans 10:14.

Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn about, to convert; Acts 26:18.

Hebrew pethach (H6608) — an opening, an entrance; Psalm 119:130.

Hebrew pethiy (H6612) — simple, open-minded; Psalm 119:130.

Usage

"“how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Rom 10:14) — the Hanover mission in a question."

"“to turn them from darkness to light” (Act 26:18) — the commission, with no exemptions."

"“The entrance of thy words giveth light” (Psa 119:130) — why he taught reading."
